concepts.definition: A match is two 45-minute halves, and the clock never stops for fouls or the ball going out.
concepts.exampleLine: "It's ninety minutes and the clock doesn't stop, so nobody's ever really out of it."

concepts.definition: Extra minutes the referee adds at the end of each half to make up for time lost to goals, injuries and delays.
concepts.exampleLine: "Six minutes added on and they're still throwing bodies forward."

concepts.definition: A goal counts when the whole ball crosses the whole goal line between the posts and under the crossbar.
concepts.exampleLine: "Whole ball over the line, or it's not a goal."

concepts.definition: The ball is out when all of it crosses a touchline or goal line, or the referee stops the game.
concepts.exampleLine: "It's the whole ball over the line, not just a bit of it."

concepts.definition: Restart from the touchline for the team that did not touch the ball last, taken with both hands over the head.
concepts.exampleLine: "That's their throw, it came off our player last."

concepts.definition: Restart taken by the defending team from its own six-yard box after the attackers put the ball over the goal line.
concepts.exampleLine: "Quick goal kick, they've all pushed up."

concepts.definition: Restart from the corner arc when the defenders put the ball over their own goal line; you can score directly from it.
concepts.exampleLine: "We get a corner every time we push them back, and that's where we're dangerous."

concepts.definition: A direct free kick can score straight away; an indirect one must touch another player first.
concepts.exampleLine: "That's an indirect one, so he can't just shoot it straight in."

concepts.definition: A one-on-one shot from 12 yards awarded for a foul by a defender inside their own penalty area.
concepts.exampleLine: "That's a penalty, the foul was inside the box."

concepts.definition: Knockout ties level after 90 minutes go to two 15-minute periods, then a penalty shootout if still level.
concepts.exampleLine: "It'll go to penalties, I can't watch."

concepts.definition: Some knockout rounds are played home and away; the combined score decides it, and away goals no longer count double.
concepts.exampleLine: "It's 2-1 on aggregate, so they only need one goal in the second leg."

concepts.definition: A league win earns three points, a draw one and a loss none; the table is ranked on points.
concepts.exampleLine: "A draw feels like a loss when you're chasing the title."

concepts.definition: A match in which a team concedes no goals.
concepts.exampleLine: "Fourth clean sheet in a row, that back four is locked in."

concepts.definition: Three goals by one player in a match is a hat-trick; two is a brace.
concepts.exampleLine: "He got a hat-trick in the first half, absolutely ridiculous."

concepts.definition: The penalty area, six-yard box, penalty spot, centre circle and halfway line frame most of the rules.
concepts.exampleLine: "He fouled him just inside the eighteen-yard box."

concepts.definition: Each side starts 11 players; leagues typically allow five substitutions in three windows plus half-time.
concepts.exampleLine: "Making a double change at the hour mark, he's trying to change the game."

concepts.definition: One player per team wears the armband, speaks to the referee and represents the team.
concepts.exampleLine: "Only the captain is supposed to talk to the ref."

concepts.definition: Careless, reckless or excessive-force contact such as a kick, trip, push or charge gets a direct free kick or a penalty.
concepts.exampleLine: "That was a clear foul, he got nothing of the ball."

concepts.definition: A caution for unsporting behaviour, dissent, persistent fouls or tactical fouls; two yellows in a match mean a red.
concepts.exampleLine: "He's on a yellow already so he has to be careful."

concepts.definition: A sending-off for serious foul play, violent conduct, denying a goal-scoring chance or a second yellow; the team plays a man down.
concepts.exampleLine: "Down to ten men for the whole second half, that's game over."

concepts.definition: The referee lets play continue after a foul if the fouled team benefits, and can go back for the foul if it does not.
concepts.exampleLine: "Great advantage, the ref let him run on."

concepts.definition: Fouling an attacker who had a clear goal chance is a red card, or a yellow if it is a penalty and the defender challenged for the ball.
concepts.exampleLine: "Last man, DOGSO, straight red."

concepts.definition: Deliberately touching the ball with hand or arm, or making the body unnaturally bigger, is an offence; the shoulder is not the arm.
concepts.exampleLine: "His arm was out, natural position or not, that's the debate."

concepts.definition: Pretending to be fouled to win a free kick or penalty is a yellow card offence.
concepts.exampleLine: "He went down way too easily, that's a dive."

concepts.definition: A referee, two assistants on the touchlines, a fourth official at the bench and video officials in a room.
concepts.exampleLine: "The assistant flagged, the ref went to the monitor."

concepts.definition: Defenders must stand at least 9.15 m (10 yards) from the ball at a free kick, usually lined up as a wall.
concepts.exampleLine: "Look how far back they've made the wall stand."

concepts.definition: A goalkeeper may not handle the ball if a teammate deliberately kicks it to him, or throws it in directly to him.
concepts.exampleLine: "He has to use his feet there, he can't pick that up."

concepts.definition: A goalkeeper who holds the ball longer than eight seconds concedes a corner, with a visible five-second countdown at the end.
concepts.exampleLine: "He's holding it too long, the ref's counting down with his hand."

concepts.definition: From 2026/27: a five-second visual countdown on delayed throw-ins and goal kicks, then possession or a corner goes to the other side.
concepts.exampleLine: "They're stalling but the ref's got the countdown up now."

concepts.definition: Arguing with or abusing the referee is a yellow card offence; leagues now stress captain-only conversations.
concepts.exampleLine: "That's a yellow for dissent, you can't shout at the ref."

concepts.definition: Stopping a promising counter with a deliberate foul, usually for a yellow, to break the momentum.
concepts.exampleLine: "Great tactical foul, he took the yellow to stop the counter."

concepts.definition: A player treated on the pitch must stay off for at least one minute after play restarts, under the 2026/27 clarification.
concepts.exampleLine: "He has to go off for a minute after treatment now."

concepts.definition: The only player allowed to handle the ball in open play (inside their own penalty area), and the last line of defence.
concepts.exampleLine: "The keeper had a monster game, three saves in one-on-ones."

concepts.definition: A central defender who marks strikers, wins headers and organises the defensive line.
concepts.exampleLine: "He's a proper old-school centre-back, all timing and heading."

concepts.definition: A wide defender on the left or right who defends the flank and often overlaps to attack.
concepts.exampleLine: "Our right-back gets forward more than the winger."

concepts.definition: A wide player in a back-three system who covers the whole flank, attacking and defending.
concepts.exampleLine: "In a back five the wing-backs do double the running."

concepts.definition: A midfielder who sits in front of the defence to break up play and start attacks.
concepts.exampleLine: "We need a proper six, someone to screen the back line."

concepts.definition: A midfielder who links defence and attack and covers a lot of ground.
concepts.exampleLine: "He's the engine, an eight who does everything."

concepts.definition: A creative player just behind the striker who unlocks defences with passes.
concepts.exampleLine: "He's our number ten, everything goes through him."

concepts.definition: A wide attacker who beats full-backs, crosses or cuts inside to shoot.
concepts.exampleLine: "Their winger destroyed our full-back all night."

concepts.definition: The main goalscorer who leads the line, finishes chances and holds up the ball.
concepts.exampleLine: "He's a proper nine, lives in the six-yard box."

concepts.definition: A centre-forward who drops deep into midfield to drag defenders out of position and create space for others.
concepts.exampleLine: "He plays as a false nine so he's always dropping in."

concepts.definition: A midfielder who defends his own area and arrives late to attack the other.
concepts.exampleLine: "He covered every blade of grass, a proper box-to-box player."

concepts.definition: A player, often deep, who sets the tempo and finds the key pass.
concepts.exampleLine: "He's the metronome, the whole team plays through him."

concepts.definition: A striker whose game is being in the right place in the box for tap-ins and rebounds.
concepts.exampleLine: "He's a poacher, nothing fancy, just always there."

concepts.definition: A goalkeeper who plays far off his line, sweeping up through balls and joining the build-up with his feet.
concepts.exampleLine: "Sweeper-keeper, he's basically an extra outfield player."

concepts.definition: Traditional numbers hint at roles: 1 keeper, 2-5 defenders, 6-8 midfield, 10 creator, 9 striker, 7 and 11 wingers.
concepts.exampleLine: "He wears the 10 for a reason."

concepts.definition: Teams are ranked by points, then goal difference and other tiebreakers set by each league.
concepts.exampleLine: "We're third but only on goal difference."

concepts.definition: In most of the world the bottom teams drop down a division each season and the top of the lower one goes up.
concepts.exampleLine: "Three go down every year and it gets brutal at the bottom."

concepts.definition: A knockout competition inside one country, such as the FA Cup, where small clubs can face giants.
concepts.exampleLine: "It's the cup, so anything can happen."

concepts.definition: UEFA runs the Champions League, Europa League and Conference League; qualification depends on league position.
concepts.exampleLine: "We need top four for the Champions League next season."

concepts.definition: Fixed periods, usually summer and January, when clubs can register new players.
concepts.exampleLine: "It's deadline day, everything's happening."

concepts.definition: A club buys a player's contract for a fee, or borrows him for a season on loan, sometimes with an option to buy.
concepts.exampleLine: "He's out on loan with an option to buy."

concepts.definition: A player in the last months of a contract can negotiate with other clubs and leave for free when it ends.
concepts.exampleLine: "His contract's up in the summer so he can go for free."

concepts.definition: A club's youth system that develops players who might reach the first team or be sold.
concepts.exampleLine: "He came through the academy, proper local lad."

concepts.definition: The manager picks the team and tactics; the sporting director or head of football runs recruitment and long-term planning.
concepts.exampleLine: "The manager wanted him but the sporting director wouldn't pay the fee."

concepts.definition: Leagues limit spending with rules such as the Premier League's squad-cost rule, UEFA's squad cost ratio or the MLS salary cap.
concepts.exampleLine: "They got a points deduction for breaking the spending rules."

concepts.definition: A match between local rivals with extra history, noise and emotion.
concepts.exampleLine: "It's a derby, throw the form book out."

concepts.definition: Chants, banners (tifo), ultras and supporters' trusts are part of a club's identity, and owners sometimes clash with fans over them.
concepts.exampleLine: "The atmosphere was unreal, the whole end sang for ninety minutes."

concepts.definition: An attacker is in an offside position if any part of the head, body or feet is nearer the opponents' goal line than both the ball and the second-last opponent.
concepts.exampleLine: "His shoulder was ahead of the last defender."

concepts.definition: Being in an offside position is not an offence; it becomes one only when you play or touch the ball, or interfere as a teammate passes.
concepts.exampleLine: "Offside position, but he never touched it so no offence."

concepts.definition: An attacker level with the second-last defender is onside; the benefit of the doubt goes to the attacker.
concepts.exampleLine: "Level is onside, so it stands."

concepts.definition: Offside applies only if the player interferes with play, interferes with an opponent, or gains an advantage from the position.
concepts.exampleLine: "He stood offside but he wasn't involved in the play."

concepts.definition: Head, body and feet count for offside; hands and arms (down to the bottom of the armpit) do not.
concepts.exampleLine: "Arms don't count, but his knee was past the line."

concepts.definition: If a defender deliberately plays the ball, the attacker who receives it is not offside; a deflection or block does not reset it.
concepts.exampleLine: "It was a deflection, not a deliberate play, so he was still offside."

concepts.definition: You cannot be offside from a throw-in, goal kick or corner kick.
concepts.exampleLine: "Can't be offside from a corner, so the goal stands."

concepts.definition: Video assistant referees can only intervene for goals, penalties, direct red cards and mistaken identity, and only for a clear and obvious error.
concepts.exampleLine: "VAR only steps in for a clear and obvious error."

concepts.definition: VAR checks every incident silently; a review means the referee looks at a pitchside monitor or accepts advice.
concepts.exampleLine: "They've gone to the monitor, that's a review."

concepts.definition: Tracking cameras and limb data build a 3D offside line and animation in seconds, replacing hand-drawn lines.
concepts.exampleLine: "The graphic came out in about twenty seconds."

concepts.definition: VAR may now correct clearly wrong second yellows and mistaken identity, and review wrongly awarded corners where it can be done immediately.
concepts.exampleLine: "They can review a corner now, but only if it's quick."

concepts.definition: A defensive line steps up together at the moment of the pass to catch attackers offside.
concepts.exampleLine: "That's the trap, the whole back line stepped up together."

concepts.definition: Fans argue over thin margins, and over proposals like the daylight rule where the attacker must be fully clear.
concepts.exampleLine: "Daylight offside would end the toenail goals, but it would change the game."

concepts.definition: 4-3-3 lists outfield players from defence to attack; the numbers count each line, not exact spots.
concepts.exampleLine: "We play a 4-2-3-1, so four at the back and one striker."

concepts.definition: A defence of two centre-backs and two full-backs; the most common structure.
concepts.exampleLine: "A flat back four is easier to coordinate."

concepts.definition: Three centre-backs with wing-backs, letting the team overload midfield or cover wide areas.
concepts.exampleLine: "A back three gives us an extra body to win the ball."

concepts.definition: Four defenders, three central midfielders and a front three of two wingers and a striker.
concepts.exampleLine: "Our 4-3-3 stretches teams with the wingers hugging the touchlines."

concepts.definition: Four defenders, two holding midfielders, three attacking players behind a lone striker.
concepts.exampleLine: "In a 4-2-3-1 the ten sits behind the nine."

concepts.definition: Two banks of four with two strikers up front; compact and simple.
concepts.exampleLine: "4-4-2 is two banks of four, really hard to break down."

concepts.definition: Teams shift shape: a 4-3-3 with the ball can become a 4-5-1 without it, or a 3-2-5 with full-backs tucked in.
concepts.exampleLine: "They look like a 4-3-3 but they build in a 3-2-5."

concepts.definition: Keeping gaps between lines and players small so the opposition has no space between them.
concepts.exampleLine: "They stayed compact, there were no gaps to play into."

concepts.definition: Attackers stretch the pitch sideways (width) and forwards and backwards (depth) to pull the defence apart.
concepts.exampleLine: "Width on the wing, depth from the striker, that's how you open a defence."

concepts.definition: The vertical channels between the wide and central areas, a favourite place for creators to receive the ball.
concepts.exampleLine: "He lives in the half-space, between the full-back and centre-back."

concepts.definition: The space between a defence's back line and its midfield line, where a turning attacker is dangerous.
concepts.exampleLine: "He got the ball between the lines and turned."

concepts.definition: Paths between teammates that are not blocked by defenders; angles create lanes.
concepts.exampleLine: "No passing lane, so he had to go back."

concepts.definition: Three players forming a triangle give the ball carrier two passing options at different angles.
concepts.exampleLine: "Triangles everywhere, they always have an easy pass on."

concepts.definition: Putting more players than the opponent has into one zone to create a free man.
concepts.exampleLine: "We overloaded the left and the right winger was free on the switch."

concepts.definition: A quick long pass from one flank to the other to attack the weak side.
concepts.exampleLine: "The switch was perfect, the winger had acres of space."

concepts.definition: How a team moves the ball from the goalkeeper through the thirds to create a shot.
concepts.exampleLine: "They build up patiently from the back."

concepts.definition: Goalkeeper and defenders pass short to escape pressure and draw opponents forward; risky but rewarding.
concepts.exampleLine: "Risky to play out from the back but when it works it's beautiful."

concepts.definition: A pass that moves the ball meaningfully closer to the opponent's goal.
concepts.exampleLine: "He plays progressive passes, always looking forward."

concepts.definition: A pass into the space behind the defence for a runner.
concepts.exampleLine: "Lovely through ball, he split the defence."

concepts.definition: A cross is a ball from the wide area into the box; a cutback is a low pass from near the byline back towards the edge of the box.
concepts.exampleLine: "The cutback was better than the cross because it beats the keeper's line."

concepts.definition: A teammate runs outside (overlap) or inside (underlap) the ball carrier to give options and drag defenders.
concepts.exampleLine: "The full-back overlapped and the winger went inside."

concepts.definition: A pass to a teammate that sets up a pass to a third player running into space.
concepts.exampleLine: "That third-man run beat the whole line."

concepts.definition: Closing down opponents quickly to win the ball back or force a bad pass.
concepts.exampleLine: "They press like mad, high up the pitch."

concepts.definition: A cue, such as a back pass, a bad touch or a pass to the touchline, that tells the team to press together.
concepts.exampleLine: "The back pass was the trigger and they all went."

concepts.definition: Pressing in the opposition half to win the ball close to goal.
concepts.exampleLine: "High press, and they scored within six seconds of winning it."

concepts.definition: Defending in the middle third, letting the opponent have the ball in their own half, then pressing when it enters your zone.
concepts.exampleLine: "We sat in a mid-block and waited."

concepts.definition: Defending deep with narrow lines to protect the box and hit on the counter; sometimes called parking the bus.
concepts.exampleLine: "They parked the bus and nicked one on the break."

concepts.definition: Pressing immediately after losing the ball to win it back before the opponent can organise.
concepts.exampleLine: "Counter-press, they won it back in five seconds."

concepts.definition: A fast attack after winning the ball while the opponent is out of shape.
concepts.exampleLine: "Lightning counter, three passes and it was in the net."

concepts.definition: Defenders stand far up the pitch, squeezing space but leaving room behind them.
concepts.exampleLine: "They hold a really high line, so one ball over the top hurts."

concepts.definition: Zonal defenders guard areas; man-markers follow a specific opponent.
concepts.exampleLine: "Are they zonal or man-marking at corners?"

concepts.definition: The players who stay back while others attack, ready to stop counters.
concepts.exampleLine: "Great rest defence, he was back to snuff it out."

concepts.definition: Leaving one pass open to lure the ball into a zone, then closing it, often near the touchline.
concepts.exampleLine: "They forced him toward the touchline, the trap worked."

concepts.definition: Speeding up or slowing the game deliberately; keeping possession is not the same as controlling the game.
concepts.exampleLine: "They had 70 percent possession but no control."

concepts.definition: A rehearsed plan for a corner: where players start, who runs where and the delivery type.
concepts.exampleLine: "They had a routine, the near-post flick was planned."

concepts.definition: An inswinger curls toward goal; an outswinger curls away from it.
concepts.exampleLine: "Inswinger from the right, keepers hate those."

concepts.definition: The near post is the one closer to the taker; runs and flick-ons attack different posts.
concepts.exampleLine: "He flicked it on at the near post and someone tapped in at the far."

concepts.definition: Teams defend corners with zonal, man or hybrid systems, often leaving a couple of players on the posts.
concepts.exampleLine: "They switched to hybrid marking after conceding three corner goals."

concepts.definition: A corner played short to a teammate to change the angle and pull defenders out.
concepts.exampleLine: "Short corner, that pulled the marker away."

concepts.definition: Attackers legally shield the keeper's or a marker's path; obstruction is the fine line.
concepts.exampleLine: "It was a legal screen, not a foul."

concepts.definition: Direct free kicks use dip, curve and dead-ball strikes around or over a wall; delivery is often crossed for headers.
concepts.exampleLine: "He bent it round the wall, in the top corner."

concepts.definition: Takers pick a corner or a cheeky chip (the Panenka); keepers study habits and dive early or wait.
concepts.exampleLine: "The keeper waited and saved it."

concepts.definition: Teams alternate five kicks each (ending early if one side cannot catch up), then sudden death; a coin toss decides who goes first.
concepts.exampleLine: "It's a shootout, five each and then sudden death."

concepts.definition: The loose ball after a clearance or flick-on, where set-piece chaos becomes a goal.
concepts.exampleLine: "Set pieces are all about the second ball."

concepts.definition: A throw-in launched into the box like a cross, a weapon for some teams.
concepts.exampleLine: "Their long throw is basically a corner."

concepts.definition: A short-passing, high-possession style built on triangles and patient movement, made famous by Barcelona and Spain.
concepts.exampleLine: "It's tiki-taka, endless passing until the gap opens."

concepts.definition: A system (juego de posición) where players occupy zones so the ball carrier always has options; associated with Cruyff and Guardiola.
concepts.exampleLine: "It's not passing for passing's sake, it's positional play."

concepts.definition: A fluid 1970s Dutch idea where any player can take any role and the shape stays balanced.
concepts.exampleLine: "Total football, everyone rotates."

concepts.definition: An Italian, defence-first system with a sweeper and strict marking, built to win 1-0.
concepts.exampleLine: "Catenaccio was the original park-the-bus."

concepts.definition: The German term for counter-pressing, popularised by Klopp: the best playmaker is the turnover close to goal.
concepts.exampleLine: "Klopp said gegenpressing is the best playmaker."

concepts.definition: A full-back who steps into midfield when his team has the ball to overload the centre.
concepts.exampleLine: "The right-back tucks inside, he's an inverted full-back."

concepts.definition: A style that goes long and early, using target men, second balls and set pieces.
concepts.exampleLine: "They play direct, a lot of long balls and second balls."

concepts.definition: A long-running argument between attractive possession football and results-first pragmatism.
concepts.exampleLine: "Is it winning ugly or is it pragmatism?"

concepts.definition: A build-up shape where the full-backs move inside to join two central midfielders, forming a four-player box in midfield.
concepts.exampleLine: "City build in a box in midfield, with the full-backs inside."

concepts.definition: A shot-quality number: the probability a shot becomes a goal, based on distance, angle and situation.
concepts.exampleLine: "We lost 1-0 but won the xG 2.1 to 0.3."

concepts.definition: The combined xG of the shots a player's passes set up, measuring chance creation independent of the finishing.
concepts.exampleLine: "His xA is great even if the strikers keep missing."

concepts.definition: Passes allowed per defensive action, a rough gauge of pressing intensity; lower means more pressing.
concepts.exampleLine: "Their PPDA is under eight, that's a heavy press."

concepts.definition: The share of time a team holds the ball; it says nothing about quality or danger by itself.
concepts.exampleLine: "Sixty percent possession but not one shot on target."

concepts.definition: A dribble that moves the ball meaningfully towards goal; a data measure of ball-carrying.
concepts.exampleLine: "He leads the league in progressive carries."

concepts.definition: Shots on target force a save or go in; the ratio hints at finishing and shot selection.
concepts.exampleLine: "Twenty shots but only two on target, shooting from everywhere."

concepts.definition: Goals scored minus goals conceded, the first tiebreaker in many leagues.
concepts.exampleLine: "We're level on points but their goal difference is better."

concepts.definition: Scoring well above xG is likely unsustainable; regression towards the mean is a common analyst point.
concepts.exampleLine: "He's overperforming his xG so it won't last."

concepts.definition: Fans debate whether numbers or watching matches tells you more; the best takes use both.
concepts.exampleLine: "The data says he's great but the eye test disagrees."

concepts.definition: A quick way to compare teams over different numbers of matches or the last five games.
concepts.exampleLine: "They're averaging better than two points a game, that's proper contender form."

concepts.definition: Held every four years since 1930 (paused for the Second World War); Brazil have won five, Argentina won 2022 and Spain won 2026.
concepts.exampleLine: "Brazil has five stars, Argentina won 2022 and Spain took 2026."

concepts.definition: The first with 48 teams, hosted by the USA, Canada and Mexico; Spain beat Argentina 1-0 after extra time in the final.
concepts.exampleLine: "The 2026 final went to extra time and Ferran Torres won it for Spain."

concepts.definition: The annual award for the best player, given by France Football; arguments over who deserves it are endless.
concepts.exampleLine: "He deserved the Ballon d'Or with that season."

concepts.definition: Messi vs Ronaldo vs Pelé vs Maradona: an argument about how to weigh trophies, style, longevity and era.
concepts.exampleLine: "The GOAT debate is basically about what you value."

concepts.definition: El Clásico, the Manchester derby, the North London derby and the Old Firm carry decades of history.
concepts.exampleLine: "It's not just three points, it's the derby."

concepts.definition: A 1995 ruling that let players move for free at contract end, transforming transfer markets and wages.
concepts.exampleLine: "Bosman changed everything, players finally had power."

concepts.definition: England's top tier became the Premier League in 1992, a commercial league with huge global TV deals.
concepts.exampleLine: "The Premier League turned football into a global TV product."

concepts.definition: England's FA banned women's football on affiliated grounds from 1921 to 1971; the 1999 World Cup and the NWSL's 2013 launch fed a modern boom.
concepts.exampleLine: "The ban lasted fifty years and look at the crowds now."

concepts.definition: The NASL and Pelé in the 1970s, the 1994 World Cup, MLS in 1996, Beckham in 2007 and Messi in 2023 mark US soccer's growth.
concepts.exampleLine: "MLS started in 1996 after the World Cup in the USA."

concepts.definition: Arsenal's unbeaten 2003-04 league season and Manchester United's 1999 treble are benchmark achievements.
concepts.exampleLine: "Unbeaten all season, that's the Invincibles."

concepts.definition: League position (and some cup wins) decides Champions League, Europa League and Conference League places.
concepts.exampleLine: "Top five gets Champions League if England earns the extra place."

concepts.definition: England's historic knockout cup, open to clubs from the Premier League down to non-league.
concepts.exampleLine: "It's the FA Cup, the magic of the cup."

concepts.definition: Spain's top league, dominated by Real Madrid and Barcelona, with Atlético Madrid as the usual challenger.
concepts.exampleLine: "Clásico weekend is basically a holiday."

concepts.definition: A closed league of franchise clubs with a salary cap, Designated Players, no relegation and playoffs after the regular season.
concepts.exampleLine: "There's no relegation in MLS, so mid-table isn't dangerous."

concepts.definition: The Shield goes to the best regular-season team; MLS Cup is decided in the playoffs.
concepts.exampleLine: "They won the Shield but lost in the playoffs."

concepts.definition: MLS plays a short transition season in early 2027, then moves to an August-to-May calendar in 2027-28.
concepts.exampleLine: "MLS is moving to the European calendar in 2027."

concepts.definition: The US women's top league has no relegation, a playoff decides the champion, and the Shield goes to the top regular-season team.
concepts.exampleLine: "Gotham won it as the lowest seed in 2025."

concepts.definition: 36 clubs play eight different opponents in one table; the top eight go straight to the last 16 and 9-24 enter playoffs.
concepts.exampleLine: "Top eight skips the playoff round, that's the whole race."

concepts.definition: Twelve groups of four; the top two plus the eight best third-placed teams reach a round of 32.
concepts.exampleLine: "Third place can still go through with the new format."

concepts.definition: Players represent nations in tournaments and qualifiers, with international breaks pausing the club calendar.
concepts.exampleLine: "It's an international break so no club games."

concepts.definition: Too many matches in a short span forces rotation, injuries and tired legs.
concepts.exampleLine: "They're playing three games a week, of course they're tired."

concepts.definition: A club-season pause for national-team games, when injuries and travel matter.
concepts.exampleLine: "Everyone's holding their breath for the international break."

concepts.definition: Availability news (out, doubtful, back in training) shapes team selection and fan mood.
concepts.exampleLine: "He's doubtful, he trained yesterday."

concepts.definition: Shorthand made famous by reporter Fabrizio Romano: a transfer is confirmed and essentially done.
concepts.exampleLine: "Romano posted here we go, it's done."

concepts.definition: When results dip, fans and media speculate about a manager being fired; boards weigh cost, timing and fit.
concepts.exampleLine: "Two points from six, he's under pressure."

concepts.definition: The fight between the top teams, where goal difference, head-to-heads and the run-in matter.
concepts.exampleLine: "It's a three-horse race and the run-in is brutal."

concepts.definition: Teams near the bottom fight for survival; points gaps and games in hand define the drama.
concepts.exampleLine: "It's a relegation scrap, every point is huge."

concepts.definition: The final stretch of the league season when fixtures and pressure decide everything.
concepts.exampleLine: "The run-in is the hard part."

concepts.definition: A spectacular goal, from long range or an improbable angle.
concepts.exampleLine: "That was a worldie, top bins."

concepts.definition: A nutmeg is passing the ball between an opponent's legs; a rabona is a kick with the kicking foot crossed behind the standing leg.
concepts.exampleLine: "He nutmegged him and did a rabona in the same move."

concepts.definition: A fan phrase for collapsing under pressure in a big moment.
concepts.exampleLine: "They bottled it, they had it wrapped up."

concepts.definition: Clinical means taking chances efficiently; wasteful means creating chances but missing them.
concepts.exampleLine: "They were clinical, one chance, one goal."

concepts.definition: A win without dominance, often praised as a sign of a champion mentality.
concepts.exampleLine: "It was ugly but three points are three points."

concepts.definition: Friendly teasing between fans; a good exchange includes respect for the other side.
concepts.exampleLine: "Fine, you win this time, but wait for the return leg."

concepts.definition: Fans talk about the decisive moment, the manager's changes and whether the result was fair.
concepts.exampleLine: "It came down to the substitution at the hour mark."

concepts.definition: The best conversational move is a genuine question about why the fan loves the team or a specific player.
concepts.exampleLine: "What was it about him that made him your favourite?"

payload.title: After a heartbreak loss
payload.setting: She texts after her team loses a derby.

exchanges.theirMessage: Ninety-eighth minute. NINETY-EIGHTH. I can't even.

replies.text: That is brutal. Which moment hurt most?
replies.theirResponse: The equaliser. We were so close.
replies.coachNote: Empathy first, then a real question.

replies.text: Ah well, it's just a game.

payload.closingNote: She is hurting; she wants empathy first and football second.

payload.title: She loves corners
payload.setting: She is excited about a corner goal.

exchanges.theirMessage: That near post flick was so well drilled!!

replies.text: Was that a planned routine? The far post man was waiting.

replies.coachNote: Corners are the opposite of luck.

payload.closingNote: She noticed a rehearsed routine, a near-post flick and a far-post tap-in.

payload.title: The offside goal
payload.setting: She is angry about a disallowed goal.

exchanges.theirMessage: Offside by a TOENAIL. Literally a toenail!

replies.text: Toenail? Do you think they should change the rule?

replies.coachNote: Don't defend tech to a fan mid-rage.

payload.closingNote: She thinks VAR was harsh; the semi-automated line said offside by a toe.

payload.title: Her team pressed high

exchanges.theirMessage: They pressed like maniacs, won it high and scored in six seconds.

replies.text: That press trigger was the back pass, right?
replies.theirResponse: Exactly! They all jump on it.

replies.text: Cool. Was it a nice goal?

payload.closingNote: She is talking about a pressing trigger and high press that won the ball in the attacking third.

payload.title: Transfer news
payload.setting: She is nervous about a star player.

exchanges.theirMessage: Apparently he's leaving in January?? Please no.

replies.text: Is it confirmed or just a rumour? I'd wait for the club statement.

payload.closingNote: She read a rumour; 'here we go' means it's real, otherwise it is speculation.

payload.title: Numbers night
payload.setting: She defends her team with xG.

exchanges.theirMessage: We lost but the xG says we won. Stats don't lie!

replies.text: Fair, but how much of that xG was the big chance he skied?
replies.theirResponse: Ha, fine, the miss was awful.
replies.coachNote: Gently engages; xG is a model.

replies.theirResponse: You didn't even try to understand.

payload.closingNote: She is using xG to argue her team was unlucky.

payload.title: Derby banter
payload.setting: She teases you about a rival.

exchanges.theirMessage: Enjoy second place while it lasts.

replies.text: Cute. Come back with the head-to-head after the derby.

payload.title: World Cup memories
payload.setting: She is reminiscing about the 2026 final.

exchanges.theirMessage: Torres in the 106th minute. I still get chills.

replies.text: That final was wild. Where did you watch it?
replies.theirResponse: With my dad at a bar!

payload.closingNote: She refers to Spain beating Argentina 1-0 in extra time.
